executive_summary: The defining thread running through today's content is the crisis of institutional trust in artificial intelligence — who controls it, who profits from it, and whether the systems governing it are honest. The Musk v. Altman trial, now reduced to a credibility contest between two men whose personal ambitions may shape the future of OpenAI, is not merely a legal dispute but a referendum on whether the most consequential technology in a generation will be governed by accountability or ego. The Polymarket insider trading story reported in the New York Times reinforces this same anxiety from a different angle: prediction markets built on data integrity are themselves being gamed, suggesting that even the tools designed to surface truth are vulnerable to manipulation by those with privileged access. The Economist's scrutiny of data center backlash and MIT Technology Review's assessment of Google's diminished standing in the foundation model race add further dimension, revealing an industry that is simultaneously expanding its physical and competitive footprint while losing the public and institutional confidence needed to do so responsibly. Taken together, today's content makes clear that the central question of this technological moment is not capability — it is credibility.

newsletters.title: 🔴 Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?

items.headline: Inside Tech: Is the backlash against data centres justified?
items.blurb: A year ago I reported on the impact of artificial intelligence on the fight against climate change. On the one hand, data centres used a lot of electricity; on the other, that electricity was mostly renewable, and could be used to develop technologies that helped cut emissions around the world. Overall it felt like cause for cautious optimism, especially if—as we argued in an accompanying leader—AI companies would share more information about the impact of their systems to help consumers make informed decisions. A lot has changed since then. Some shifts were predictable. The amount of electricity the AI industry uses has exploded. The biggest models take more energy to train and run than they did last year, and they are being used by more people to do more things more of the time. Some adjustments were grimly inevitable. Where big tech companies once felt bound by promises they had made in a different political era to cut, or even reverse, their emissions, they now seem happy to switch on new gas turbines to power their growing ambitions, although they still generally insist that the extra energy use is just a temporary measure to compensate for a lack of capacity on the electricity grid. Other changes were more surprising. Last year data-centre impacts felt like a niche topic discussed by people interested in the overlap between AI and climate change. Now they are an increasingly important part of national—and international—politics. In America politicians are proposing regional and national moratoriums on construction, prompting entrepreneurs to wonder whether it might be cheaper to launch computers into space rather than fight through the morass on Earth.

longform.title: Musk v. Altman week 3: now the jury will pick a side
longform.thesis: The final week of the Musk v. Altman trial reduced to a credibility contest between two men whose personal ambitions — Altman's alleged self-dealing and Musk's alleged AGI power-grab — are now central to how courts and the public will adjudicate the future governance of OpenAI.
longform.context: This newsletter dispatch covers the third and final week of the Musk v. Altman trial, in which Elon Musk sued Sam Altman and OpenAI over the organization's contested transition away from its nonprofit founding mission. The piece arrives as the case moves to jury deliberation, making the outcome imminent and consequential.
arguments: Altman's credibility was attacked by Musk's lawyers on grounds of lying and self-dealing, framing him as an executive who exploited OpenAI's nonprofit structure for personal gain rather than its stated mission of safe, broadly beneficial AGI development.

Musk was counter-portrayed by OpenAI's defense as a 'power-seeker trying to control artificial general intelligence,' with the trial surfacing evidence — including a golden trophy of a donkey's ass awarded to an employee who challenged Musk — that depicted him as autocratic and retaliatory rather than principled.

The trial 'unearthed new details about OpenAI's contested nonprofit status,' suggesting that the legal proceedings have produced a public record about OpenAI's governance and mission drift that extends beyond the personal dispute between the two founders.
longform.significance: The jury's verdict will set a legal and reputational precedent for how nonprofit AI organizations can convert to for-profit structures, directly affecting OpenAI's ongoing restructuring. The trial has also forced into the public record competing narratives about who bears responsibility for AI governance failures at the most influential AI lab in the world. At a moment when AGI timelines are shortening and regulatory frameworks remain thin, the outcome shapes both institutional accountability and public trust in AI leadership.
questions_raised: Whether the jury's credibility determination — Altman as self-dealer versus Musk as power-seeker — will translate into a legal finding that actually constrains OpenAI's for-profit conversion, or merely produce reputational damage without structural consequence.

What the trial's newly surfaced details about OpenAI's nonprofit status mean for the California and Delaware attorneys general oversight processes already scrutinizing the conversion, and whether this litigation accelerates or complicates that regulatory review.

longform.title: What to expect from Google this week
longform.thesis: Google enters its 2026 I/O developer conference as a clear third-place finisher in the foundation model race, particularly in coding, while retaining a genuine competitive edge in AI for science that will likely be overshadowed by its more visible weaknesses.
longform.context: Author Grace Huckins writes as a preview piece on the eve of Google I/O 2026, framing the conference against a backdrop of Google's deteriorating standing in AI coding relative to Anthropic's Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex, a decline sharp enough that DeepMind engineers reportedly had to be permitted to use a competitor's tool to remain productive.
arguments: Google's coding capabilities have fallen so far behind Anthropic and OpenAI that the company reportedly allowed some DeepMind engineers to use Claude Code — a competitive product — for internal work, signaling an operational crisis rather than merely a product gap. Huckins anticipates a major coding release (potentially an update to the 'Antigravity' agentic platform) but explicitly tempers expectations: 'Unless the company has made astonishing progress since then, Google probably won't make it back to the coding frontier in the next two days.'

AI for science remains Google's 'conspicuous strength' and the one domain where it holds a durable frontier advantage: the company is the only frontier AI lab to have earned a Nobel Prize, and tools like the AI co-scientist (described as an 'oracle' by a Stanford scientist) and AlphaEvolve demonstrate sustained R&D depth that rivals cannot easily replicate. Huckins argues these announcements 'might receive less attention, but they will be no less consequential.'

Google's health AI posture illustrates a strategic ambiguity — the company is releasing its Health Coach publicly but positioning it around fitness and diet advice rather than clinical concerns, raising the question Huckins poses directly: 'Is this another area where Google has fallen behind, or is the company exercising appropriate caution in a high-stakes domain?' This framing identifies health AI as a second competitive front where Google trails OpenAI's narrative dominance since ChatGPT Health launched in January 2026.

Google faces internal political pressure that complicates its public neutrality: 600 employees, many from DeepMind, signed a protest letter to CEO Sundar Pichai over a pending DoD contract, which Google signed the following day. While Demis Hassabis has avoided the public CEO feuds characterizing rivals, Huckins notes that 'controversies will worm their way in regardless,' testing whether Google can 'maintain its veneer of neutrality' on stage.
longform.significance: The piece matters because it maps a concrete competitive hierarchy in the foundation model race at a moment — mid-2026 — when the rankings have stabilized enough that even internal Google behavior (borrowing a competitor's coding tool) confirms them. It also surfaces a structural tension in how AI capability leadership is now defined: coding benchmarks dominate reputational rankings even as domain-specific scientific AI may deliver more consequential real-world impact, a prioritization Huckins implicitly challenges. The employee protest over DoD contracts signals that AI labs' national-security entanglements are becoming a recurring fault line within the companies themselves, not just in public policy debates.
questions_raised: Whether Google's caution in health AI — deploying a tool focused on fitness rather than clinical medicine — reflects genuine safety discipline or competitive timidity, and whether that distinction will matter to regulators and users evaluating the responsible deployment of medical AI.

Whether Google's durable lead in scientific AI (Nobel-backed, institutionally deep) will ever translate into the kind of market and reputational dominance that coding benchmarks currently confer, or whether the field's definition of 'frontier' will continue to disadvantage Google despite its strongest research outputs.
